bio.en: Geoff Charles is VP of Product at Ramp, the fastest-growing SaaS business in history, which reached over $100 million in annual run rate within two years using a team of roughly 50 people.
bio.zh: Geoff Charles 是 Ramp 的产品副总裁；Ramp 是史上增长最快的 SaaS 公司，用约 50 人的团队在两年内达到超 1 亿美元年化经常性收入。

summary.en: Geoff offers a unique glimpse into Ramp's velocity-obsessed operating model: tiny teams (sometimes three engineers) that ship competitors to public companies in months and move billions of dollars a year. He explains how they operationalize a culture of speed through first-principles thinking and strong individual empowerment, how they organize planning and define strategy, and how they interview PMs while keeping an extremely high talent bar. He also addresses the real risk of burnout in such a fast culture and how to avoid it.
summary.zh: Geoff 带我们一窥 Ramp 以速度为核心的运营模式：极小的团队（有时仅三名工程师）能在几个月内做出上市竞品的对手产品，并每年流转数十亿美元。他解释了他们如何通过第一性原理思考和充分授权，把速度文化落到日常；如何组织规划、定义战略；以及如何在保持极高人才标准的同时面试 PM。他也谈到了这种高速文化下真实的倦怠风险，以及如何避免它。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. So you mentioned it, you nailed it. Velocity is everything at Ramp. It's how we design our product development process. It's how we incentivize teams, it's who we want to hire, it's who we want to promote, and it's everything around how we make decisions and how we organize the organization. (00:07:43): I think it came from the fact that during the pandemic, we started with a very small team and there was a huge market opportunity ahead of us and it wasn't so much which path we wanted to pick, but rather how fast we were able to execute on that path. And so velocity was ingrained from the early days on just building, shipping, and iterating. And I think it's a decent metric for how companies and teams perform. You might say, "Well, what's the impact of that velocity?" But realistically, teams that have high velocity are able to actually get to that impact over time by iterating. It's also a great way to have positive selection in terms of talent because talent wants to join companies that ship fast. And a lot of people who join Ramp, I ask them, "Why are you interested in joining the company?" And they often say, "Well, it's because you guys are actually building things and shipping things and I want to know what that feels like." And it's also a great way just de-risk decisions and decision making. If the cost of that decision is really low, then you're able to essentially simplify a lot of decisions.
turns.zh: 是的，完全赞同。你提到了这一点，一针见血。速度就是Ramp的一切。它是我们设计产品开发流程的方式，是激励团队的手段，是我们招聘和晋升人才的标准，更是我们做决策和组织架构的核心理念。（00:07:43）：这源于疫情期间的经历。当时我们团队规模很小，但市场机遇巨大，关键不在于选择哪条路，而在于能否快速行动。自早期阶段起，我们就深深根植于快速构建、快速上线、快速迭代的文化中。我认为速度是衡量公司和团队绩效的绝佳指标。你可能会问：“但速度对业绩有何实际影响？”但现实是，高速度团队通过持续迭代，最终能逐步释放其价值。它也是吸引人才的有效手段，因为人才渴望加入能快速交付成果的公司。许多加入Ramp的人都会问：“为何对加入我们感兴趣？”他们常答：“因为你们真正在开发产品、上线服务，我想亲身感受这种快感。”速度还能降低决策风险——当决策成本极低时，决策过程就能被简化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To build on that, there's a lot of companies that say they move fast, that talk about moving fast, that say velocity is really important, moving fast is really important to us, but I feel like Ramp is very different from that, where it's actually incredibly, incredibly fast and it's actually something you come back to again and again, this idea of, how do we move faster? Can you just share an example or two of what velocity actually looks like at Ramp and what the reality of that is?
turns.zh: 接下来，许多公司都声称行动迅速，强调速度至关重要，但Ramp的速度远超常规。我们以极快的速度行动，屡屡突破挑战。比如，我们在三个月内打造了与Amex竞争的平台；六个月后又推出与Expensify竞争的产品（这两家都是上市公司）；年营收突破1亿美元。当时研发部门仅50人，四名工程师和三名产品经理。随后我们进军应付账款领域，仅用三个月就完成了Bill.com竞争产品的开发（三名工程师、一名设计师、一名产品经理），成果惊艳，产品年交易额达数十亿美元。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Yeah. So when I joined, we were about 10-ish folks, about eight engineers, and in three months, we built a competitor to Amex. Six months after that, we built a competitor to Expensify, both publicly traded companies. We hit a hundred million in annual revenue. I think we were under at that point 50 total in the R&D department, less than four engineers and three PMs. And then we started expanding into accounts payable. We basically gave a team goal of building a competitor, Bill.com. It was three engineers, one designer, one PM three months, and they hit out of the park. And that product is moving in billions of dollars a year. (00:09:49): And I think the recipe for all this is constantly small teams have a single-threaded focus, give them the resources they need to execute big lofty goals, very tight timelines, and then shield them from the chaos that is the rest of the organization. So basically don't bother them and don't even tell the rest of the company that you're doing these things until they find product market fit, until they actually find that early traction and then they can bring in more resources. So it's like gravity and you need gravitational pull to this thing.
turns.zh: 秘诀在于：小团队专注单一目标，赋予他们实现宏伟目标所需资源，设定紧凑的时间线，并将其与组织的其他混乱部分隔离开来。简单来说，直到产品找到市场契合点、获得初期反馈后，再让其他部门介入资源支持。这就像重力吸引物体，速度就是引力场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I want to double click on some of these points you just made. So what you find is important to help teams and people move fast within Ramp is you talked about single-threaded teams, shielding them from other people, trying to pull them in different directions, lofty goals. There's a couple more things. Let's talk about the single-threaded piece a little bit. What does actually mean? What does that look like?
turns.zh: 好的。我想再深入探讨一下你刚才提到的几个要点。你发现，要帮助团队和成员在Ramp平台上快速推进，关键在于打造单线程团队，避免他们被其他人或各种分心事物拖累，无法专注于宏伟目标。接下来还有几个方面需要讨论。先来谈谈单线程团队的概念。具体来说，什么意思？这又该如何落地？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: There are very few people who are able to execute extremely well in more than one thing, and it's especially true for individual contributors. And so what I mean by single threaded is there's only one goal, one thread, that they're waking up in the morning to focus on. And in order to remove that, you basically need to remove anything else that they're being asked to do to just focus on that thing, whether it's any type of research or any type of production engineering or any type of process that's outside of that single goal. And it almost goes as far as just saving a room in the office just for them and they are just in that room all day every day just working on that one thing.
turns.zh: 很少有人能同时在多个领域表现出色，尤其是个人贡献者更是如此。所谓单线程团队，就是指团队成员每天早上醒来后，只需专注于一个目标、一条主线即可。为了实现这一目标，必须排除所有其他可能分散注意力的工作，比如研究、生产工程或与单一目标无关的流程。甚至可以为他们专门划出一个办公室，让他们整日专注于手头任务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's an example of that? Either maybe someone's working on it now or in the past that's a good example of a single-threaded goal or team.
turns.zh: 能举个例子吗？比如现在或过去有没有人团队或个人能体现单线程目标的典范？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Yeah. So, for example, we launched a flex product over the last summer, that was a single-threaded team just focused on eCommerce companies and their needs with more cash flow conversion and cash flow smoothing. And so we kept that team again just purely focused on just shipping that product and hitting that goal. And if they were ever distracted by something else, I don't think we would've hit it.

turns.en: How do you, as a leader, avoid distracting them knowing there's so many things you need to do and there's constantly this like, "Oh, if we just fix this one bug, this one customer is going to be so happy," and, "Okay, if I just ask this one PM to work on this for a day?" I know there's not going to be like, "Here's the rule of step one, two, three, but how do you actually approach shielding teams from things that just are constantly on fire?
turns.zh: 作为领导者，如何避免分散他们的注意力？毕竟有太多事情需要处理，总会有人说“只要修复这个漏洞，客户就会很开心”，或者“让我请产品经理处理一天这个任务”。显然不可能制定一套固定的规则，但如何有效保护团队免受各种紧急事务的干扰呢？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: So, for example, on bugs or issues like that, we have individuals that are protecting those teams from those issues. So we have a rotational program on production engineering, for example, where engineers are protecting the core team from escalations, from bugs, from issues. We have product operators that are protecting the PM from the chaos that is documentation and escalations and release management and enablement customer requests. So we have layers of protective tissue to core teams, but I would say for any of these big bets, you basically have to pull folks from different teams and reorganize a sub-team. And that team typically doesn't have responsibility on any existing product because these are all fairly new products. I think it gets more challenging when you go from one to two rather than zero to one.
turns.zh: 比如针对漏洞或问题，我们有专门的人员为团队排除这些干扰。例如，生产工程团队实行轮班制，工程师负责保护核心团队免受升级请求、漏洞和问题的困扰。产品运营团队则负责处理文档、升级请求、发布管理和客户支持等事务，为核心团队构建防护网。但对于重大项目，通常需要从不同团队抽调人员，重组子团队。这些团队通常不负责现有产品，因为这些都是新项目。在从一个项目到两个项目的过渡中，挑战会更大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You also mentioned this idea of lofty goals and that's something I've seen a lot. At Airbnb, there was a ... It is very known for lofty goals. Brian was famous for going to meetings where people present their goals and their plans and he's like, "How do we 10X that? What do you need in order to 10X that goal?" And then that ends up being your goal and often works shockingly, sometimes burnt a lot of people out. How do you think about for just finding that balance and, I don't know, is there an example of just like, "Here's a really ambitious goal?" Or maybe the question is just, how do you find the balance of ambitious but not just impossible?
turns.zh: 你还提到了设定宏伟目标的这个理念，我对此深有体会。在Airbnb，公司以宏伟目标著称。布莱恩以在会议上提问而闻名——当人们展示自己的目标和计划时，他总会反问：“我们如何能让这个目标翻十倍？要实现这个目标需要什么？” 最终，这些目标就成了团队的行动指南。虽然这种方法有时会让团队承受巨大压力，但最终效果往往令人惊叹。不过，有时也会让团队成员精疲力竭。你如何看待这种平衡呢？有没有具体的例子可以说明如何设定一个既雄心勃勃又切实可行的目标？或者说，这个问题本质上在于如何在雄心与现实之间找到平衡？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Yeah. So the first thing is we have market comparables, which is very exciting for us. So when you look at Bill.com, they're a publicly traded company, Expensify, publicly traded, or Concur or Coupa, these are all large players that are actually very motivating and largely de-risk some of the business decisions you're making. That's existing markets. We've also been able to create markets. Spend management was an actual market before we and other competitors jump into it. (00:14:18): So that's motivating. Go attack that market and go drive that revenue is very motivating. We also use designs as a way to motivate teams. So we spend a lot of time with designers crafting out what the future of this thing could look like and that's also extremely motivating. So we constantly go back to these cornerstone, Loom walkthroughs of Figma prototypes that the design spend a lot of time talking through and I think that's a big part of the motivation. And so both of those things combined, I think, helps us stay motivated. I think there's a constant pushback to like, "Okay, what can we actually achieve?" But you're able to move super, super fast if you have those two things in mind, the market and the revenue goal, because very revenue driven as a company and the designs that can really keep you anchored on what this could look like.
turns.zh: 是的。首先，我们有市场可参照的案例，这对我们来说非常振奋人心。比如Bill.com作为上市公司，Expensify、Concur或Coupa等大型企业，它们的成功案例确实能极大地激励我们，也能为我们的商业决策降低风险。这些都是现有市场。我们还成功开拓了新市场。在我们和其他竞争对手进入之前，支出管理领域就已经是一个成熟的市场了。（00:14:18）：所以这很能激发斗志。去攻克那个市场、推动营收增长，这种动力非常强大。我们还通过设计来激励团队。比如，我们会花大量时间与设计师一起构思产品的未来形态，这也极大地激发了团队的热情。因此，我们经常回顾Loom平台上的Figma原型演示文稿，与设计团队深入探讨这些构想，我认为这正是激发团队动力的关键因素。两者结合起来，确实能让我们保持持续的积极性。当然，团队也会不断自我质疑：“我们到底能实现什么目标？” 但只要牢记市场和营收目标这两个核心指标，行动就会迅速高效，因为我们是一家以营收为核心驱动力的公司，而设计团队能有效帮助我们构想未来的可能性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know another important ingredient to how you all operate is you really like to empower product teams and give them a lot of control over how they operate and what they build and how they set goals and things like that versus micromanaging them. I think you have this concept of context over control. I'm curious how you actually operationalize that. A lot of people love the idea of empowering their teams and then they do that and then they do the wrong thing or they take too long or they set the wrong goals. So how do you actually make that work and create empowerment within your teams?
turns.zh: 我知道你们的运营模式中还有一个重要元素——你们非常重视赋予产品团队自主权，让他们自主决定运营方式、产品研发方向、目标设定等，而不是进行微观管理。我认为你们提倡“赋予上下文而非控制权”的理念。想听听你们是如何具体实践的。很多公司都想赋予团队权力，但结果却事与愿违，比如团队做错了事、效率低下、目标设定不当。你们是如何确保赋权机制有效运作的？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Yeah, it was one of the biggest cultural differences, I think, in Ramp versus other companies that were as a part of where my boss, the CTO, Karim, was extremely hands-off in terms of the actual pride decisions because we were extremely aligned on the goals themselves. And so that's where you really just start alignment is, what is the goal that you're going after? What is the hypothesis that you have to reach that goal? What is the data by which you're coming up with that hypothesis? And then what is the potential solution to test that hypothesis? And oftentimes, more junior leaders, and I was certainly in that camp earlier on, kept focusing on the solutions and debating the right solution when in fact you should really be debating upstream of that. You should be debating the interpretation of data, you should be debating the hypotheses and the different ideas that you have there as to what's really going on or you should be debating the goals themselves. (00:16:39): And so whenever things went wrong at Ramp, it was when I was being prescriptive with regards to the solution without actually explaining and aligning upstream on the goal, the hypothesis, and the data. And if you do that, you realize that the solutions actually can come much better from teams that are much closer to the ground. I think that's the biggest goal that I have now in my role is to continue giving context so that teams focus on the right goals, come up with the right hypotheses and focus on the right data points. And I spent most of my time just repeating myself, most of my time just sharing the context that I think they might be missing, especially given that I'm in certain meetings or certain groups in certain forms that they're not a part of and my responsibility to represent them and then share back the context for them to make better decisions over time.
turns.zh: 是的，这应该是Ramp与其他公司之间最大的文化差异之一。我认为，我的CTO卡里姆（Karim）在实际决策时极少插手，因为我们在目标上高度一致。真正的共识始于：我们要追寻的目标是什么？达成这个目标需要哪些假设？这些假设基于哪些数据？然后又该如何验证这些假设？很多初级管理者——我自己早期也曾深陷其中——往往过于关注解决方案，争论正确的方案，而实际上更应该在上游进行探讨。比如，应该如何解读数据？如何验证假设？如何剖析背后的深层逻辑？或者直接讨论目标本身。（00:16:39）在Ramp遇到问题时，往往是因为我过于偏重解决方案，却没有提前与团队达成共识。如果能提前明确目标、假设和数据，团队自然能提出更优的解决方案。我现在工作的核心目标就是持续提供上下文，让团队专注于正确的目标、假设和数据点。我大部分时间都在重复强调这些观点，尤其是在某些会议或团队中，他们并不知情，而我的职责就是代表他们传达信息，帮助他们做出更明智的决策。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That touches on a phrase that's come up a couple times on this podcast that a leader's job, you're essentially the repeater in chief, reminding people of strategy, vision, things like that. It feels like to move fast, you need to do what you're talking about, which is empower your teams to just move, otherwise, it's not scalable. And I'm curious just to make it even more real. Either ... Is there an version of something you did at your previous work versus at Ramp that just shows what that looks like when you're empowering your team and not in the weeds? What's most different there? Is it the product reviews, you're not as involved in design iterations? Where do you come in to actually give feedback? How does that actually look like working at a Ramp versus another company?
turns.zh: 这让我想起播客中多次提到的观点：领导者的职责本质上是充当首席重复者，不断提醒团队战略、愿景等内容。想要快速推进，必须让团队自主行动，否则无法实现规模化。我很好奇能否具体举例说明。比如，与之前的工作相比，Ramp有哪些不同之处？是产品评审阶段？你是否不参与设计迭代？你如何提供反馈？与其他公司相比，Ramp的工作模式有何独特之处？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: I think that the contract between me and the team is really their strategy and their roadmap. And as long as we are aligned on the strategy, and we can get into that, and aligned on the roadmap and the timing, that's their contract. And so then at that point, my goal is to continue to give them context to execute on that and to coach them through that by getting firsthand data on how things are going that they might be missing. And their role is to highlight risks and highlight one-way decisions that they need my input on. And, again, it didn't use to start that way. I mean, when we first started, it was just me and another PM. I was fairly micromanaging in some areas. I think you build trust over time and you start having these contracts. And so as, I suppose, good more senior, they're basically publishing out the API by which they interact with me and we basically align on what's most important on each one on one. (00:19:09): So I basically have teams ... All my directs post their goals every week first thing Monday. The goal there is to also have them review each other's goals. I have a one-on-one template that I basically use to keep on track of how progress is being made, but I certainly don't spend the time in the one on one going into that. I spend the one on one just focusing on what they need from me. And then on a biweekly basis, I have a team-wide meeting where I share context that everyone is missing and we go deep on the most important topics of the day.
turns.zh: 我认为我和团队之间的合同实际上是他们的战略和路线图。只要我们在战略上保持一致，能够深入探讨路线图和时间节点，这就构成了我们的合同。在这种情况下，我的目标是持续为他们提供执行所需的背景信息，通过获取他们可能忽视的实时数据来指导他们。他们的职责是指出风险并强调需要我参与决策的单向决策。当然，事情一开始并非如此。刚开始时，只有我和另一位产品经理。我在某些领域管得过细。我认为信任是逐步建立的，最终形成了这样的合作模式。（00:19:09）：所以我基本上让团队……所有直接下属每周一早晨第一时间提交他们的目标。目标还包括互相评审彼此的计划。我有一个一对一沟通模板，用于跟踪进展情况，但一对一会议中我不会详细讨论这些内容，而是专注于他们需要我提供的支持。每两周，我会召开全团队会议，分享大家可能忽视的关键信息，并深入探讨当天最重要的议题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What about the product experience itself? Is there design review that happens? How do you stay on top of just like, "I'm proud of this product that we're shipping as a team?"
turns.zh: 那产品体验本身呢？是否有设计评审环节？你们如何确保团队能为自己推出的产品感到自豪？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: I'd say we're iterating. I think when the first couple of years, it was more asynchronous and ad hoc process. And once you hit 10, 15 PMs and 20 or 30 different mini pods shipping constantly, I think you need a bit more of a process by which you have high-risk decisions that are being surfaced. So we're iterating. I think we're relating now is any large rock that we have on the roadmap needs to be brought into the product review process, where myself and the head of design are present and giving feedback, but it needs to be structured in a way where you are asking specifically for what type of feedback you need and you're highlighting the key risks and tradeoffs that you're making implicitly in that review. (00:20:38): So that's one way we're able to scale, but I would say largely people ship and it's the difference between a beta and the GA, that's where we really get plugged in. When we make the decision to go live to the rest of the customer base and asking sales to start selling, that's where I'll really come in and stress test the hypotheses and the decisions. It's further downstream so it's more risky, but because we move so fast, you don't waste that much time if you have to pull it back.
turns.zh: 我认为我们一直在改进。最初的几年里，流程比较分散和临时。但当团队发展到10、15名产品经理，加上20、30个不同的小团队持续上线产品时，我们需要更规范的流程来识别高风险决策。现在我们在改进，比如路线图上的每个重大项目都必须纳入产品评审流程，由我和设计总监共同参与并提供反馈。但流程需要结构化，要明确需要什么样的反馈，并突出评审中隐含的关键风险和权衡取舍。（00:20:38）：这就是我们实现规模化的一种方式，但我认为大部分工作都是由团队完成的。GA（正式发布）和Beta（测试版）之间的区别很重要，真正需要我们介入的阶段是决定向所有客户群上线，并让销售团队开始推广产品时。这时我会深入测试假设和决策，风险更高，但因为我们的速度很快，如果需要调整，也不会浪费太多时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that came up actually. I just had a chat with Nicole Forsgren, who's world expert on developer productivity and developer experience, and they've done all this research on quality and speed of engineering and the engineering team. And they find that quality goes up as your product velocity goes up. You'd think it'd be the opposite. The faster you move, the lower quality ends up being. But exactly to your point, because you can fix things really quickly and you can get things out the door and there's not this huge chunk you have to wait for people to review and release and break things, ends up being higher quality. So it's very much aligned with our experience.
turns.zh: 是的，这个问题确实被提出来了。我刚和妮可·福斯格伦聊过，她是开发者生产力和开发者体验方面的世界级专家。他们对工程团队的质量和速度进行了大量研究，发现随着产品开发速度的提升，质量也会随之提高。你可能会觉得情况相反——速度越快，质量越低。但正如你所指出的，因为你能快速修复问题、快速发布产品，又不必等待漫长的评审和发布流程，等待问题暴露的时间更短，最终质量反而更高。这与我们的经验非常吻合。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Yeah. And you have to create a system by which those folks are getting that feedback. And so we've really focused on what are the control mechanisms that ensure that your high velocity doesn't tank the business. And so examples of that is we have a voice of customer processes where every single negative review that is shared to our products is shared back to the tech lead, the PM and the designer on a monthly basis. We report back NPS and CSAT. We report back operational overhead, meaning the percentage of tickets that come from your product area normalized by the number of users that are using that product. And that's a core contract that the team has to maintain a low or lower part of operational burden. We also have bugs and issues being directly assigned to the engineer that's on call. So they feel that pain and then they can continue, to your point, leveraging velocity to solve those problems. Velocity is just a magnitude, it's not necessarily a specific direction.
turns.zh: 是的。你必须建立一个系统，让这些团队成员能获得反馈。因此，我们特别关注了哪些控制机制能确保高速度不会损害业务。举例来说，我们有一套“客户之声”流程，每月会将用户对产品的负面评价反馈给技术负责人、产品经理和设计师。我们会汇报净推荐值（NPS）和客户满意度（CSAT），还有运营开销数据，即产品领域的工单量占使用该产品的用户数量的比例。这是团队必须维持的核心契约，要求运营负担保持在较低水平。我们还会将漏洞和问题直接分配给值班工程师，这样他们就能切身感受到问题带来的压力，进而按照你的说法利用速度优势解决这些问题。速度只是个量级，不一定指向某个特定方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With these bugs that are coming in and quality issues versus a team's goal and their KPIs that they're trying to hit, how do you recommend teams balance those two things?
turns.zh: 对于这些漏洞和质量问题，如何平衡与团队目标及关键绩效指标（KPI）的关系？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: We don't have a bug backlog. We fix every bug once they're surfaced almost.
turns.zh: 我们没有漏洞积压问题。几乎所有漏洞一经发现就会立即修复。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: So it's part of the production engineer's job really just to fix those things. I think where we get to nuances, like user experience improvements, the metric there that I really look at is how many support tickets come in that were due to a customer being confused. So we track that. And if that number is slightly elevated, we're basically saying, "You can't ship any new features, you need to fix these things." And so, yeah, there's just these types of controls, but basically trying to standardize across the teams. This is your percentage of operational burden, this is your CSAT, this is your NPS, and this is the number of customers that are confused. As long as you maintain those metrics, you can do whatever you want. But the moment that these things are under the red, you can't ship new features and you need to revert back to the [inaudible 00:24:03].
turns.zh: 所以，修复这些问题是生产工程师的职责所在。在用户体验改进这类细微层面，我特别关注的指标是因用户困惑而产生的支持工单数量。我们会追踪这一数据。如果该数字略有上升，我们就会明确表示：“不能上线任何新功能，你们必须先解决这些问题。”总之，团队需要遵守这些控制机制，比如运营负担率、CSAT、NPS，以及用户困惑率等指标。只要这些指标保持正常，团队可以随意推进新功能。但一旦这些指标触红线，就必须暂停新功能上线，并回归到之前的流程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something funny that happened after our post on how Ramp builds product came out, someone on LinkedIn, a product manager, posted half-jokingly that her CEO came to her and every PM CEO came to them after that post. And they're just like, "How do we prioritize velocity? How do we move faster? Look at this, this culture of velocity that Ramp's got, why don't we have that? What do we need to create this culture of velocity?" And I worried a little bit because it creates this additional pressure on product managers that already have a really hard job with already a lot of pressure. So I was like, "Oh, man, we're creating this new pressure that this one company is doing things really well and now everyone has to do it this way." So I guess my question is just, what's your advice to product managers who are getting this push from leaders to move faster as a result of how you guys operate?
turns.zh: 关于我们发布的Ramp如何打造产品的文章引发热议后，LinkedIn上一位产品经理半开玩笑地发帖称，自那篇文章发布后，她的CEO找她谈话，随后其他产品经理的CEO也纷纷找他们讨论同一个话题：“我们该如何优先考虑开发速度？如何加快进度？看看Ramp的这种‘速度文化’，我们为什么没有呢？要如何打造这样的‘速度文化’？” 这让我有点担忧，因为这无形中给本就压力重重的产品经理们增添了额外压力。当时我就在想：“天哪，我们又制造了一个新压力源——某家公司做得特别好，现在所有人都得照着他们的模式来。”所以我想问问各位，面对领导层因Ramp的成功而施加的这种加快进度的压力，产品经理们该如何应对？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Yeah. Well, one, I'm sorry. It goes without saying. PMs, we can't do anything by ourselves. We're very useless. We're force multiplier. So the one thing that I'll highlight is behind Ramp's velocity is a lot less the culture that I try to amplify, but a lot more the quality of the engineering and design talent candidly. And so I'm just standing really on their shoulders here. And so advice number one is ensure that from the top down there's an investment in R7D as a first-class citizen that you're paying upmarket, that you're hiring the best, that you're focusing on your engineering and tech brand, that you're bringing people who want to work there because they want to be empowered. And then you have a culture of empowerment. And what that means is ... And it's hard to get right. What that means is the CEO has less say in the product that is built and the engineers have a lot more say into it. (00:25:48): And so it's something that I've seen done really, really well at Ramp where the CEO sets the vision but is much less opinionated about the specific sequence by which we get there and trusts a tech organization that is radically empowered. The second thing that I would say is the biggest waste of time is meetings and status updates. And I think that oftentimes CEOs would say, or leaders would say, "Hey, we've got increased velocity, therefore let's just add these status meetings and let's add all this process and all these documents and all these ways to hold teams accountable." And that's just a huge way to demotivate people. And so I've never had a status meeting. I've never scheduled a status meeting. Statuses are done async. They are done in the systems by which they operate and largely they should be in real time. And meetings should be all about collaboration, ideation, decision-making, et cetera. So just look at your calendar and just kill as many things as possible and kill just unimportant process. (00:26:56): And the last thing that I would say is oftentimes leaders say, "I want to move super fast," but they'll say, "I want everything under the sun. I want this and that and that." An example of that at Ramp is always like the debate between adding more products to one segment or going to a different segment, SME versus mid-market versus enterprise. And you ask the CEO, "Hey, which one should we do?" And they would say, "All of it," because they think that the more goals you have, the faster you'll be able to execute. And I think there's just a limitation to that. (00:27:29): So the thing I would amplify is be very clear with the tradeoffs that you need to make and present those tradeoffs back to your leadership team. So here's what we're doing and here's what we're not doing and why and which one would you pick? Give them a menu of items. And you'll see that you're able to execute much, much faster on four things rather than eight at the same time. That's your job. Your job is to basically communicate those tradeoffs that oftentimes are not well communicated to executives out of fear of looking like you're pushing back. You're actually not pushing back, you're increasing velocity.
turns.zh: 是的。首先，我很抱歉。这是不言而喻的。关于产品管理（PMs），我们无法独自完成任何事情。我们非常无能。我们是力量倍增器。所以我想强调的一点是，Ramp的开发速度背后，与其说是我试图放大的一种文化，不如说是工程和设计人才的卓越质量。说实话，我只是站在他们的肩膀上而已。因此，我的第一个建议是，从上到下要确保将R7D视为一级公民进行投资——给予高薪，招募最优秀的人才，专注于工程和技术品牌，吸引那些渴望获得授权的人才加入。然后你就拥有了一种赋权文化。这意味着……而这很难做到。具体来说，CEO对最终产品的控制权应该更少，工程师对产品的控制权应该更多。（00:25:48）：我见过Ramp在这方面做得非常出色，CEO设定愿景，但对实现愿景的具体步骤几乎不加干预，而是信任一个被赋予了极大权力的技术团队。我的第二个观点是，会议和状态更新是最浪费时间的。我认为很多CEO或领导者会说：“嘿，我们提高了开发速度，所以让我们增加状态更新会议，增加流程和文档，加强团队问责。”但这只会极大地打击员工积极性。我从未参加过状态更新会议，也从未安排过状态更新会议。状态更新都是异步完成的，在团队运营的系统中进行，并且应该实时更新。会议应该专注于协作、构思和决策等。所以看看你的日程表，尽可能减少不重要的流程。（00:26:56）：最后，我想说，很多领导者会说：“我想快速推进，但我又想做这做那。”以Ramp为例，经常会讨论是向一个细分市场添加更多产品，还是转向不同的细分市场——中小企业、中端市场还是企业客户。当你问CEO：“我们该选哪个？”他们会说：“全都要”，因为他们认为目标越多，执行速度越快。但我认为这存在局限性。（00:27:29）：所以我要强调的是，要清晰传达需要做出的权衡，并向领导团队展示这些权衡。例如，我们要做什么，不做什么，以及原因。然后让他们选择。这样比同时做八件事要高效得多。这就是你的职责。你的职责是向高管传达这些权衡，而高管们往往因害怕显得反抗而避而不谈。但你其实不是在反抗，而是在提升效率。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm hearing from a meta point you're making is use that ask as leverage to change the way things are operating. Is that right?
turns.zh: 从更宏观的角度来看，你的意思是利用这种提问来改变现有运作方式。对吗？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: 100%. You can't ask for velocity and not have empowerment and not trust and not eliminate process and not increase the focus. And that requires some serious tradeoffs that oftentimes leaders, especially those coming from more traditional industries, are not comfortable with. And it was the biggest breath of fresh air when I joined Ramp was how committed the team was. (00:28:33): The last thing I'll say is there's nothing more motivating than a leader just commenting, "This is awesome," on a random project channel at a random design crit. I know that our founders are just reading the projects that they actually care a lot about and the engineers know that. And so there's just a general excitement on just building great cool shit. And engineers just feel that and they're also highly motivated by that. So that's another piece of advice is just being able to stay plugged in to give engineers the opportunity to present to those leaders present in the all hands. That's also a great way to amplify the culture.
turns.zh: 100%。你不能只要求高效率，却不重视赋能、缺乏信任、忽视流程优化以及不增强专注力。这需要做出重大取舍，而许多领导者——尤其是那些来自传统行业的领导者——往往难以接受这样的挑战。当我加入Ramp时，团队的高度投入感无疑是一股清新之风。（00:28:33）：最后我想说的是，没有什么比得上领导者在随机设计评审会上随口称赞“这太棒了”更能激发团队斗志。我知道我们的创始人会仔细阅读他们真正关心的项目，而工程师们也深知这一点。因此，团队对打造酷炫产品的热情简直无与伦比。工程师们能真切感受到这种激情，也因此充满动力。所以我的另一个建议是，要保持与团队的紧密沟通，让工程师有机会在全体会议上向在场领导汇报成果。这也是弘扬企业文化的绝佳方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a good segue to this idea of burnout. Hearing a team operate incredibly fast and velocity, velocity, velocity makes you think about, are people burning out? Are they enjoying their work? How are they sustainably going to last at Ramp? I'm curious just what that's like and how you think about avoiding burnout for folks that are just constantly shipping, shipping, shipping.
turns.zh: 这正好引出关于职业倦怠的讨论。听说一个团队以极高的效率运作时，人们会不禁担忧：员工是否在透支精力？他们是否享受工作？他们如何在Ramp长久保持高效？我很好奇这种快节奏的工作环境下如何避免职业倦怠，以及如何让持续交付成果的团队保持积极性。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: I think the debate around working hard and burnout misses a key point, which is all about how much impact and how good you feel about the work that you're doing. And I think that for me, when I felt burnout, it was actually at the time where I had the lowest amount of velocity. But it was when I felt like I was putting a lot of effort into things that weren't actually moving. And so I actually think velocity is a way to potentially avoid burnout. I'm not asking people to work endless hours a week. I'm asking people to get out of their own way and to focus on what truly matters, which is building great products for our customers. And I think you do that if you get into a flow state, if you get into a cadence where everything becomes easier, where work can really become thrilling. (00:30:28): And I think sometimes organizations, especially as they grow, make that really hard. They make it really hard to just be in that flow state with a ton of distractions, a ton of meetings, a ton of cross-functional teams that are all asking for your attention and grabbing for attention. Another parallel of this is running. The best runners are the ones that love running and they feel like running isn't a chore, work isn't a chore. And I think as a runner, I try to evaluate that whenever we're doing something hard, that's challenging, that's exhausting. If you love what you do, you feel much better about the amount of effort you're putting into it. And work doesn't feel like work.
turns.zh: 我认为关于努力工作与职业倦怠的讨论忽略了一个关键点，那就是工作的影响力和个人成就感。我个人经历过职业倦怠，那是在我效率最低的时期。但当时我发现自己在投入大量精力于毫无进展的项目上。因此，我认为高效率实际上是避免职业倦怠的有效途径。我不是要求人们每周工作无休止，而是希望他们能摆脱自我束缚，专注于真正重要的事情——为客户打造优质产品。如果能进入心流状态，一切都会变得顺理成章，工作也会变得充满乐趣。（00:30:28）：有时，随着企业发展壮大，保持这种心流状态愈发困难。各种干扰、层出不穷的会议、跨职能团队的争相抢夺注意力……这些都让心流状态难以维系。跑步也是如此。最优秀的跑者热爱跑步，他们不会把跑步视为负担。作为跑者，我每次挑战高难度任务时，都会审视自己的热情。如果你热爱所做之事，就会更享受付出的过程，工作也就不再是工作了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I find the same thing. I find that when I think back to the times that had the best experience, the most fulfilling work that I've done, it's often I was working insane hours. It was just like this very long stressful project but ends up ... Looking back, you're always like, "Wow, that was so much, that was so cool. I learned so much. We shipped so much interesting stuff, made so much impact." I think the key is what you said is that you have to actually be proud of it and it has to be something that's meaningful to you because you could work long hours on something that you have no interest in and that does not help and that does lead to burnout. So that's the key.
turns.zh: 我也发现了同样的现象。当我回想那些拥有最佳体验、最有成就感的工作时，往往是在我投入疯狂工作时间的时候。比如那些漫长而充满压力的项目，最终却收获满满……回首往事，你总会感叹：“哇，那真是太棒了，太酷了。我学到了很多东西。我们推出了那么多有趣的产品，产生了重大影响。” 我认为关键在于你提到的，你必须为此感到自豪，而且这份工作必须对你有意义。因为如果你为自己毫无兴趣的事情投入大量时间，那既无济于事，还会导致职业倦怠。所以这才是关键所在。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: And you said something there, which is meaningful to you. So not meaningful to your boss or your boss's boss's boss, but meaningful to you. And I think that that's the role of management is to make everyone on your team feel like it's their goal. And the way to do that is to, again, align on that goal and give it to them and to problems to solve. If everyone feels like it's their team, it's their company, their mini company, then they will radically avoid burnout. But if they feel like the work is being pushed onto them, they feel like they're not aligned on the goal or they don't feel empowered with the solution, then the burnout will absolutely happen.
turns.zh: 你之前提到过，这份工作对你来说是有意义的。不是对你老板或老板的老板有意义，而是对你自己有意义。我认为管理者的职责就是让团队中的每个人都觉得这份工作是他们的目标。要做到这一点，首先要与团队达成共识，将目标清晰传达给他们，并赋予他们解决问题的权力。如果每个人都觉得这是属于他们自己的团队、公司或小型事业，他们就能有效避免职业倦怠。但如果他们觉得工作是被强加给他们的，或者觉得与目标不一致、缺乏解决问题的自主权，那么职业倦怠必然会发生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of my favorite quotes that you have shared is, any second you spend planning is a second you don't spend doing. And on the one hand, I love that because the more you do, the more things happen, the more you get done, everything's happening. On the other hand, it also feels a bit chaotic and I'm curious how you find that balance between, "Okay, we're not going to spend all this time planning, we're just going to go, go, go, go, go." And just how you think about that balance and how it actually ends up working out at Ramp sounds like not spending a ton of time planning.
turns.zh: 你分享过的一句我最喜欢的名言是：“用于规划的每一秒，都是你没有用于行动的每一秒。” 一方面，我很赞同这句话，因为你行动越多，事情进展越顺利，成果越丰硕，一切都在向前推进。但另一方面，这也让人感觉有些混乱。我很好奇你是如何在“好吧，我们不花太多时间规划，就直接行动行动行动行动行动行动”之间找到平衡的，以及在 Ramp 公司是如何通过这种方式实现平衡的，听起来似乎并不花太多时间在规划上。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Yeah. I would say when new joiners come at Ramp, I intro myself and I talk about our product strategy. And in the meeting with an apology, I say, "You signed an implicit contract joining Ramp. It's one where we prioritize velocity over almost everything else. What that means is it'll be somewhat chaotic. We'll ship things that don't work. We will change our products without necessarily fully enabling you and you'll have to constantly be on your toes whenever you load up a demo instance." And I think that it's an expectation and people are welcoming of that because they understand that the tradeoff is that we don't move forward, that we don't actually innovate, that we don't continue to provide value for our customers. (00:33:41): I think there's certain things that we plan for. And so the question really is because accuracy has cost, make sure that you're only increasing the accuracy of planning for the things that have high value of that accuracy. (00:33:56): And so those things for us are large market moments where we have products, marketing, and sales all coordinating these big moments. And those typically happen maybe once a quarter, once every six months. It's basically your marketing calendar. We need a plan for that, for sure, but it's oftentimes a low percentage of our total R&D focus. And so it's totally fine for each team to be somewhat autonomous, somewhat chaotic within their pod. They're extremely clear, but for the outside in, it might be very chaotic. But be very accurate on the things that truly, truly matter. The rest actually doesn't matter. You don't need a lot of accuracy and confidence on when specifically certain features will be live. It's much better to spend whatever time you would spend trying to create accuracy and creating velocity.
turns.zh: 是的。我会说当新员工加入Ramp时，我会自我介绍并谈论我们的产品战略。在会议上道歉时，我会说：“你签署了一份加入Ramp的隐含合同。在这个合同中，我们将速度置于几乎所有其他事物之上。意味着这里会有些混乱。我们会推出有问题的功能。我们会更改产品，但不一定会完全让你们跟上进度，你们每次加载演示实例时都必须保持警惕。” 我认为这是一种预期，而人们对此也乐见其成，因为他们明白这种权衡是必要的，否则我们就无法前进、创新、为客户创造价值。（00:33:41）：我们确实会为某些事情制定计划。关键问题在于准确性是有代价的，因此要确保你只在对准确性要求极高的事情上提高规划准确性。（00:33:56）：对我们来说，这些事情就是大型市场机遇，产品、市场和销售部门会为这些重大时刻通力协作。这些机遇通常每季度或每半年出现一次，这基本上就是你的营销日历。我们当然需要为此制定计划，但这通常只占我们整个研发投入的很小一部分。因此，各团队在自己的小组内保持一定的自主性和一定的混乱状态是完全没问题的。他们内部清晰明了，但对外部而言可能非常混乱。但对于真正至关重要的事情，要确保准确无误。其他事情其实无关紧要。你不需要对某些功能何时上线有过高的准确性和信心度。把用来追求准确性的时间用来提升速度要好得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you set expectations very clearly upfront. That seems really important to be successful at a company like that. It also just makes me remember every successful startup is extremely chaotic. As much as it may not feel like that on the outside, it's insanely chaotic. Things are constantly changing. I was at a fireside chat with Sheryl Sandberg once at Airbnb and somebody asked her just like, "How do you deal with change? Things are just ... We're reorging every six months. People are leaving and coming and teams are shifting and priorities are always adjusting." And she's just like, "This is the problem you want, you want to be going through this because that means you're growing and you're going through hypergrowth because the alternative is much worse where you're not growing and that's much more painful." So I think it's just a good reminder that if you're working at a place that's chaotic, it's often a good thing.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你能在前期就把预期设定得非常清楚。这对在这样的公司取得成功似乎非常重要。这也让我想起，每个成功的初创公司都极其混乱。尽管外界看不出来，但内部其实非常混乱。事情在不断变化。我曾参加过Airbnb的Sheryl Sandberg的炉边谈话，有人问她：“你如何应对变化？事情总是在变……我们每六个月就重组一次。人员离职、入职，团队不断调整，优先级也总是在变。” 她回答说：“这正是你想要的状态，你应该经历这些，因为这意味着你在成长，经历超高速增长。因为另一种情况更糟糕——你停滞不前，痛苦得多得多。” 所以我觉得这很好地提醒了我们，如果你在一个混乱的公司工作，这往往是件好事。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: I would say so. I mean, oftentimes, people use that excuse to not have a very strong strategy. And I think that for us, we've always been, from the start, the spend management platform that helps you spend less. Our strategy ... I share an annual newsletter around what we did and what we're going to do next year. And it's oftentimes pretty spot on in terms of the goals. Again, the goals and the value and the problem and the vision, that's consistent. The specifics, the timing, the quarterly scopes, all these things, yes, it changes, but what you want to avoid is the thrash of people waking up and feeling like they're working at a different company or that leaders are constantly changing their minds. We've been extremely consistent from the start and I think most of the products that we build, most of the code that we written, is in the customer's hands and hasn't been ripped away. And I think that speaks a lot to velocity, too.
turns.zh: 是的，我这么认为。我是说，人们经常用这个借口来掩饰自己缺乏清晰战略的事实。就我们而言，从一开始，我们就致力于打造一个帮助用户降低支出成本的管理平台。我们的战略……我每年都会发布一份年度通讯，回顾我们过去的成就并展望未来。通常，这些目标都相当准确。核心理念、价值主张、问题定义和愿景始终如一。具体实施方案、时间节点和季度目标等细节则会随情况变化，但最重要的是要避免让员工感到迷茫，避免领导层朝令夕改。我们从一开始就保持了高度的战略一致性，我们开发的大多数产品和编写的代码都已交付到客户手中，并且从未被轻易抛弃。这也充分体现了我们的行动效率。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That was a good addition. I didn't mean to say if your place is chaotic, it's no problem. It's that side effect of growth and hypergrowth as things are going to be pretty chaotic.
