turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Strategy means a lot of different things. In my mind, strategy is about how do we get to our goals? And it's not a roadmap and it's not a vision, it's something right in between that. So the first thing you need to do is align on what are the goals, what do you want to see in the world? Then the hypothesis, why do you think this will work? Figure out why we're uniquely positioned as a company to get after that goal. Figure out the metrics by which you would measure whether we reach that goal and then talk about the initiatives, talk about the risks, and talk about the long-term outcomes.
turns.zh: 战略涵义多样。在我看来，战略意味着我们如何达成目标。这既不是路线图，也不是愿景，而是介于两者之间的存在。首先，你需要明确目标是什么，理想的世界应该是什么样子。然后，提出假设，即你认为为什么这项战略会奏效。还要分析我们公司在实现该目标方面具有独特优势的核心原因。制定衡量目标实现情况的指标，并讨论相关举措、风险和长期影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So these are the bullet points of the contract essentially of a strategy document?
turns.zh: 这么说，这些基本上就是战略文件中的契约要点了？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Correct. And now every pod basically spends time writing that doc for themselves. So the pods are basically organized against outcomes, so they should be very clear on their goals and they publish these things out. And then what I typically do is take all these documents and make sure that they're aligned with our high-level product strategy, which is a bit more long-term thinking than the individual pods, and that they are also aligned with our financial strategy, which we can get into. But that's a little bit of how you also create a culture of empowerment where each team is thinking about these things thinking like you. And the more that, as a leader, you make teams think like you, the more leverage you get over time and the more you can start thinking ahead on other ways of operating.
turns.zh: 没错。现在每个团队基本上都在花时间为自己撰写文档。因此，这些团队基本上是围绕成果来组织工作的，因此他们应该对自己的目标非常清楚，并将这些内容公之于众。然后我通常会把所有这些文档收集起来，确保它们与我们的高层产品战略保持一致——这比各个团队的短期思考更具长远眼光——同时也与我们的财务战略保持一致——这一点我们可以详细探讨。但这也是如何营造赋权文化的方式，每个团队都在思考这些问题，并以你的思维方式来思考。作为领导者，你越能让团队像你一样思考，就能随着时间推移获得越多的影响力，并开始提前思考其他运营方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How long does planning roughly take and how often do you do this strategy rethink?
turns.zh: 规划大约需要多长时间？你们多久重新思考一次战略？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: We've gone through iterations, good and bad, I think. For a period of time at Ramp, we created OKRs with financial goals and quotas to some extent for different teams. And that led to just taking a long time to plan because people were trying to make sure there was the right metric, trying to make sure that it was achievable. And it became very political, very annoying. And largely, our entire R&D team was like, "Look, we're just going to execute on the roadmap, screw the OKRs." And so we moved from quarterly, very expensive quarterly planning, which took one month every three months, so basically 33% of the time was planning, to a biannual one-pager on, these are the company priorities and it's much more smooth and much faster. Related to that, though, we have a strong financial plan that we execute on and each row or lever of that financial plan has an owner. Oftentimes it's marketing and sales. For anything that's product led, it's product. So that's one contract. And then we have our roadmap, that's the second contract.
turns.zh: 我们经历了多次迭代，有成功也有失败。我认为在Ramp公司有一段时间，我们为不同团队制定了带有财务目标和配额的OKR。这导致规划耗时太久，因为人们试图确保指标正确、可实现，结果变得非常政治化，令人厌烦。最后，我们的整个研发团队都说：“看吧，我们还是专注于路线图吧，把OKR忘掉。”于是我们从季度规划（每三个月花一个月时间规划，相当于33%的时间用于规划）转为半年一次的简明规划，内容是公司的优先事项，这样既更顺畅又更高效。不过与此相关的是，我们有一份严格执行的财务计划，每个财务计划的行或杠杆都有负责人。这通常是市场和销售部门负责。针对产品主导的项目，则由产品团队负责。这就是一个契约。然后我们还有路线图，这是第二个契约。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of the bullet points you mentioned is this idea of being, what are we uniquely positioned to do? Can you talk a bit more about that and maybe what's an example of something you worked on, how you described why you're uniquely positioned to win at that?
turns.zh: 你提到的要点之一是，找到我们独具优势的领域。能否详细谈谈这一点，以及你曾参与的某个项目的例子，说明为什么我们在该领域具有独特的胜算？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: One of the biggest values, I think, of software is how do you reuse the components that you've built to increase, again, velocity and impact. So why we were interested in bill payments as an expansion of our corporate card platform was we saw a bill as just an invoice to the company. And an expense was an invoice to the employee. And so there was a lot of parallels between these two things. It was all about having a liability. It was all about processing that liability in terms of the financial event and moving the money, moving the money either between the company, between the company and the employee or between two companies. (00:41:38): So we believed that we were uniquely positioned to get after that space because we already had money movement. We already had some type of liability. We already integrated with accounting systems and we had a pretty strong risk process that can govern all that. And the employees that were requesting to pay these bills were already on the platform. So that's an example of a right to win. And I think that if you continue to focus on where you're uniquely positioned to win, you'll increase velocity because you already have a lot of the components of the expertise.
turns.zh: 我认为软件的最大价值之一，就是如何重用已有的组件来提升效率和影响力。因此，我们对将账单支付纳入企业卡平台的扩展业务感兴趣，是因为我们将账单视为对公司的发票，而员工的支出则相当于对员工的发票。这两者之间存在诸多相似之处——都是关于承担责任，都是要处理财务事件并转账，无论是公司内部转账、公司与员工之间转账，还是两家公司之间的转账。（00:41:38）所以我们相信，我们在该领域具有独特的优势，因为我们已经具备资金转账能力、处理责任的能力，并且与会计系统集成良好，还有一套强大的风险控制流程来监管所有业务。请求支付这些账单的员工已经在我们的平台上。这就是一个正确的战略定位案例。我认为，如果你持续专注于自己在某个领域的独特优势，就能提升效率，因为你已经拥有了大部分专业知识的组件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. It's not something you really see in teams' docs of just why we have the right to win this. So I think that's a really interesting element. By the way, I should mention we'll link to a template of your planning approach in the show notes, which we also had in the post that we worked on. So folks are trying to write down notes of all these little bullet points. We'll link to a doc that has all these things. (00:42:34): What do you think of OKRs and how do you approach OKRs as a part of this planning?
turns.zh: 这点太棒了。在团队的文档中，很少能看到关于我们为何能在这个领域胜出的清晰阐述。所以我觉得这是一个非常有趣的点。顺便说一句，我们会在节目笔记中附上你们规划方法的模板，我们之前的帖子中也提到了这一点。很多人都在努力记下这些小要点，我们会提供一个包含所有这些内容的文档链接。（00:42:34）你如何看待OKR，以及如何将OKR作为规划的一部分？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: I largely stay away from OKRs from a product perspective.
turns.zh: 从产品角度来看，我基本上避开OKR。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Go on.
turns.zh: 继续。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: I think that, again, strategy, financial plan, roadmap. I think where we landed on with OKRs were really around more cross-functional things in nature. So, for example, we'll have an OKR around winning a specific market and we'll have OKRs that are cross-functional across different teams. But, again, an OKR is just a method to measure an objective with metrics and you can use them at various levels of granularity. I stay away from them from a product perspective because, again, I want to focus on velocity, which is just output, which is your roadmap, but they're pretty strong at more of the cross-functional side of things as well as the financial side of things.
turns.zh: 我认为，再次强调，战略、财务规划、路线图。我认为我们对OKR的最终定位更多地涉及跨职能方面。比如，我们会有一个关于赢得特定市场的OKR，也会有跨团队的跨职能OKR。但同样，OKR只是用指标衡量目标的方法，你可以在不同粒度级别使用它们。从产品角度来看，我避开OKR，因为我希望专注于效率，即产出，也就是路线图，但OKR在跨职能和财务方面也非常有用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't even know what separates an OKR from not an OKR. I feel like OKRs are just a goal with some high-level statements of things we're trying to accomplish. I don't even understand when people say they use OKRs or don't, what that even means anymore. There's a recurring point on this podcast and other posts of just people are weary of just being obsessed with, "Here's the metric that we're going to hit and that's all that matters." And there's a fear they lose sight of the bigger picture, what they're trying to accomplish. But I think in the end, it's just like, "Here's what we're trying to do. Here's some goals, we're going to hit it," because I don't know care, I don't know.
turns.zh: 我甚至不知道OKR和非OKR的区别在哪里。我觉得OKR就是一个目标，附带一些高层级的陈述，说明我们要达成什么。我甚至不明白人们说他们使用OKR还是不使用OKR，这到底意味着什么。在这个播客和其他帖子中反复提到的一个观点是，人们担心只沉迷于“这是我们要达成的指标，这就是最重要的”，而忽视了更宏观的目标和愿景。但我认为归根结底，就是“这是我们要做的。这里有一些目标，我们要达成它们”，因为我不在乎，我真的不在乎。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: I think that's right. I think that's right. And at the end of the day, again, the contract is your product roadmap and that's the contract you have, the sales organization. Marketing can take that product roadmap and create market moments. And ultimately, if your product roadmap doesn't actually hit the goals of the company, then I'm accountable because I've created a system by which I've aligned with each team on why the roadmap is going to hit the goals. And so you essentially need to point back to the leader in that regard. But I can't ask every team to try to manipulate OKRs to fit their roadmaps. That's just completely exhausting. We've aligned on what we need to do, let's get it done.
turns.zh: 我觉得这没错。我觉得这没错。说到底，合同就是你们的产品路线图，而销售团队就是执行这份合同的团队。市场团队可以基于产品路线图创造市场契机。最终，如果产品路线图未能达成公司目标，那我就要担责，因为我建立了一套机制，让每个团队都清楚路线图为何能实现目标。所以在这方面，你得向领导层追责。但我不能要求每个团队都去调整OKR指标来适应他们的路线图——这实在太累人了。我们已经达成了共识，就该去把事情做好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that comes across pretty clearly in the way you think and the way Ramp operates is this idea of thinking from first principles. And it's a cliche term, feels like everyone's always trying to talk about how they're thinking from first principles and it's important to their culture to think from first principles, but it feels like you guys actually do it. And so I am curious just where that emerged for you or for Ramp. And is there an example of something that emerged within Ramp, a new product or an idea, that was very clearly from first principles?
turns.zh: 从你的思维方式和Ramp的运营方式中，可以明显感受到“从第一性原理出发思考”的理念。这是个老生常谈的术语，感觉每个人都在强调从第一性原理出发思考的重要性，但Ramp似乎真正做到了这一点。我很好奇这种理念是如何在Ramp形成的，或者有没有什么案例能体现出这种思维方式？比如Ramp推出的新产品或新创意，是否明显源自第一性原理？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: The most important thing to talk about here is that Ramp is a very unique business. I mean, we're a credit card company, which is all about risk management and underwriting. We're also a payments company because we move money between businesses. We're also a software company because we deal with spend management and expense management, accounting. We're building for SMEs. So we have PLG, but we're also building for enterprise. So we are sales driven, we're everything. (00:45:40): And so it's really important when you're dealing with something that hasn't been done before to think from first principles. And what I mean by that is you don't pattern match from your past experience, but you go back to the fundamentals of what we're trying to do and you think through them very, very deeply. And that means you need to hire people who can think from first principles and be okay putting aside their experience. And that's a tough pill to swallow for some folks who will come in and will say, "I'm the subject matter expert on X, Y, Z and I know what's best." And they come in and they get a reality check about the complexity of our business. And how also you can't influence teams by saying, "I've seen this before." That's just like an anti-pattern. You can't say, "My past company, X, Y, Z."
turns.zh:
最重要的是要说明Ramp是一家非常独特的公司。我们是一家信用卡公司，专注于风险管理和承保；同时也是一家支付公司，负责企业间资金转移；还是一家软件公司，处理支出管理和费用管理等财务事务。我们面向中小企业客户，所以采用PLG模式，但同时也为大型企业客户提供服务。因此，我们必须以销售为导向，全能型发展。

（00:45:40）：所以，当面对前所未有的问题时，从第一性原理出发思考至关重要。我的意思是，不要套用过去的经验，而是回归到我们要达成的目标的本质，进行深度思考。这就要求我们招聘能从第一性原理出发思考、愿意放下过往经验的人。这对有些人来说很难接受，他们会说：“我在X、Y、Z领域是专家，我最清楚怎么做。”但当他们加入后，很快就会意识到我们业务的复杂性，以及用“我在前公司做过类似事”这种反模式思维无法影响团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No one wants to hear that.
turns.zh: 没人愿意听这种话。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: No one wants to hear that. And surely, I thought I was coming into Ramp and I was going to apply the best product [inaudible 00:46:39] process, and I had to shift that process entirely because the process was predicated on a B-plus engineering team, and I was faced with an A-plus engineering team. And so my entire ... I had to go back to first principles around how products should be developed and built. So, again, all the advice I'm sharing here, don't just take it and map it and copy paste. Start from the first principles that we're sharing. (00:47:00): An example of that is our support team. So support reports into me. And the first principle there was saying, "Well, every support ticket is a failure of our product." We literally have that as a quote just posted on all those channels. It's a failure. And if the product works perfectly, no one should ever have to contact our support team. And what better way of holding the product team accountable for support other than having support report into product. (00:47:30): And the second piece was that we believe that a lot of our value to our customers were because it was going to come from deeply understanding them, deeply listening to them, and moving on that feedback. And so instead of hiring people who were focused just on resolving the ticket, we incentivized people to actually decrease number of tickets over time and decrease deflection or increase deflection. And that required hiring a different breed of people that then became leaders in different parts of the organization as well. (00:48:03): So, again, we could have easily just pattern matched, look at comparables, hired people who've scaled large support teams, and just used benchmarks in the industry, but we've started from first principles. And the outcome of that is we have an extremely low contact rate. We have over 400,000 users on our platform and a team of agents that's under 30. And it's a pretty crazy ratio to think about.
turns.zh: 没人想听这些。说真的，我原以为自己进入Ramp公司后，会应用最先进的产品开发流程，但后来不得不彻底调整策略，因为原有的流程是基于一个B级工程团队设计的，而我面对的却是一个A级工程团队。因此，我不得不从头开始重新思考产品应该如何开发和构建。所以，我再次强调，我在这里分享的所有建议，不要照搬照套，而是要从我们分享的基本原则出发。（00:47:00）：以我们的支持团队为例。支持团队直接向我汇报。我们的首要原则是：“每个支持工单都是我们产品存在缺陷的证据。” 我们把这句话直接贴在了所有沟通渠道上。工单的存在本身就是产品失败的证明。如果产品运行完美，就无需用户联系支持团队了。而让支持团队向产品团队汇报，正是让产品团队为支持服务负责的有效方式。（00:47:30）：第二个原则是，我们相信为客户创造价值的关键在于深入理解客户需求，倾听他们的声音，并根据反馈进行改进。因此，我们没有招聘只专注于解决工单的人员，而是激励团队成员逐步减少工单数量，降低工单转化率，并提高转化率。这就需要招聘一批不同类型的员工，他们后来也成为组织内不同领域的领导者。（00:48:03）：再说回来，我们本可以直接模仿竞争对手、参考行业标杆，招聘有过大规模支持团队管理经验的人才，但我们选择从基本原则出发。最终的成果是我们的客户联系率极低。我们平台上有超过40万用户，而支持团队却不到30人。这样的比例着实令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's wild. I missed this nuance. So the support team reports into you and the product team?
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。我忽略了这个细节。所以支持团队向你汇报，产品团队也向你汇报？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I've never heard of that. That's cool. Okay. (00:48:42): So I'm going to change course a little bit and I'm going to talk about writing. So we worked on this post together on how Ramp operates. And I was just incredibly impressed with your attention to detail, your ability to articulate, your approach to product. And as we were working on this, you mentioned that writing is really important to you as a way of figuring out what you think and to solve and crystallize problems, which is exactly how it works for me. And that's how this whole newsletter started. It was just trying to crystallize what I remembered and did so that I can remember it and share with people. So I'd love to just hear your insights and take on just what writing does for you and maybe what you'd recommend listeners do with this approach of writing, helping them think.
turns.zh: 哇，我从没听说过这种做法。太酷了。好的。（00:48:42）：接下来我要转换话题，聊聊写作。我们一起完成了关于Ramp运营模式的文章。我对你的细节关注、表达能力和产品思维印象深刻。在合作过程中，你提到写作对你来说很重要，能帮助你理清思路、解决问题、凝聚观点，这和我自己的经历如出一辙。这就是我写这份时事通讯的初衷——就是想把自己的思考和经验记录下来，方便回顾和分享。所以我很想听听你对写作的见解，以及你对听众如何运用写作思维、提升思考能力的建议。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Throughout the years at Ramp, I was often faced with a problem or a question that I couldn't answer off the bat, and I had to go back to first principles. And the best way of doing that is to shut down your laptop, take out a piece of paper, write the question as simply as possible at the top of the paper, and just spend time just thinking about how to answer that question. And there were a ton of questions over time. For example, how do we ... And it was all scalability problems that few companies have actually done successfully. And so you have to start with your own thinking, how do we scale decision making? How do we incentivize teams to work together? How do we do headcount planning? How do we allocate headcount in a fair way? How do we avoid politics as firsthand data goes away? How do we make decisions on doubling down versus pivoting? (00:50:24): All these things are really tough. And I found myself ... You could read things and that's helpful, but I don't think that reading makes you necessarily think better. It makes you more wise, but the best way to increase your capacity to think is to actually do the thinking. And so that's where I see writing. If you're able to write things clearly, you're able to think through things clearly. It was also a way for me to effectively communicate, especially during COVID, where we largely grew up during COVID, where everything was written, and it was also a way for me to get content out there to increase my brand and Ramp's brand in terms of the space that then led us to hire better people over time. So all these things worked out, but it does require you to block out time and to, again, focus on how you think about problems rather than try to Google the answer. After you thought through it, then go out and read and you'll fine-tune your thinking and you'll identify new questions to ask yourself afterwards.
turns.zh: 这些年来在Ramp工作，我经常会遇到一些一时难以解答的问题或挑战，这时我就不得不回归到基本原理。最有效的解决方法就是关掉笔记本电脑，拿出一张纸，在纸上顶端写下尽可能简洁的问题，然后花时间思考如何回答这些问题。随着时间推移，遇到的问题越来越多。例如，我们如何……这些都是可扩展性难题，很少有公司能成功解决。因此，你必须从自身思考入手：如何扩展决策能力？如何激励团队协作？如何规划人力资源？如何公平分配人力资源？如何在第一手数据缺失时避免政治化？如何在加倍投入与调整方向之间做出决策？（00:50:24）所有这些问题都极具挑战性。我发现自己……虽然阅读相关内容有所帮助，但我认为阅读并不能真正提升你的思考能力。它能让你更明智，但真正提升思考能力的方法是亲自思考。这就是我重视写作的原因。若能清晰表达自己的想法，就能清晰思考问题。这也是我在新冠疫情期间有效沟通的手段——当时我们主要通过书面交流，借此输出内容，提升个人及Ramp在行业内的影响力，最终吸引了更多优秀人才加入。这些方法确实奏效，但前提是必须腾出时间专注于问题本身，而不是一味谷歌答案。经过深思熟虑后，再去查阅资料，这样才能优化思维，发现新的探索方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this advice. You mentioned earlier that PMs can't really do much on their own, but I think this is the thing PMs can do is PMs have the time to think and to plan and think ahead because they're not required to build code all day and design. This is the advantage you have as a PM. I always think that PMs often don't really have any special unique skills. They just have the time to do the things that nobody else wants to do or doesn't have the time to do or doesn't want to do. And just this really important point of just spending the time to think and not just constantly try to discuss things in meetings or, like you said, just Google around for answers. That ends up being incredibly important. And I just love this framework of just starting a doc with a little question at the top and just sit there and try to answer the question on your own before doing anything. I think that's a really good approach. (00:52:26): I want to ask how you actually do that. How do you actually create these blocks of time? There's this concept of deep work and how valuable that is to creative work and knowledge work. How do you do that for yourself? How do you block out time and not get bugged all day?
turns.zh: 我很赞同你的建议。你之前提到产品经理单靠自己做不了太多事，但我认为产品经理能做的就是有时间思考和规划未来，因为他们无需整天编写代码或进行设计。这就是产品经理的优势。我一直觉得产品经理并没有什么特殊技能，他们只是有时间做那些别人不愿做、没时间做或不想做的事。而花时间思考而不是在会议上争论不休，或像你说的那样四处谷歌答案，这一点极其重要。我特别喜欢先在文档顶端写下一个小问题，然后独自坐下来尝试回答的框架。我认为这是一个非常好的方法。（00:52:26）我想问问你具体怎么做到的。你如何为自己创造这些专注时间？深度工作这个概念对创造性工作和知识工作非常宝贵，你是如何践行它的？你如何为自己屏蔽外界干扰，不被整天打断？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Because we're really anti-meeting at Ramp, I had time in my calendar. And so what I would basically do is the Friday before I clocked out, I would look at the next week, I would look at the top questions that I needed to spend time thinking about, and I would block out that time. I also work on one day of the weekend in terms of deep work. I find that hanging out outside and doodling on my piece of paper, some thoughts is actually really refreshing because it doesn't feel like work. It feels like just me just philosophizing about something. And so, yeah, blocking out that time, finding a space where things are less busy, where you're not in a critical path either early mornings or later afternoons or a day on the weekend is the best path for it.
turns.zh: 由于我们在 Ramp 真的很反对开会，所以我的日程表上总有空闲时间。我的做法是，在周五下班前，我会规划下周的日程，列出需要深入思考的首要问题，然后预留出专属思考时间。我还会利用周末的一天进行深度工作。比如，在户外散步、在纸上涂鸦一些想法，真的很能让人放松，因为这感觉不像是在工作，而是我在思考一些哲学问题。因此，预留出这段专属时间，在日程不那么繁忙的时段工作——无论是清晨还是傍晚，或者周末的一天——都是最佳选择。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you do if someone wants to actually schedule a meeting with you or reach out or put someone on your calendar? Do you have a policy there to protect that time?
turns.zh: 如果有人想约你开会、联系你或者把某人加到你的日程表里，你会怎么做？你有保护这段时间的政策吗？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: I think that I should never really be in the critical path of anything. So largely, I'm not available, but if they really need to get to me, they have my phone number.
turns.zh: 我觉得我永远不应该被任何事情拖入关键路径。所以大多数时候，我都是不可打扰的，但如果他们真的需要联系我，他们有我的电话号码。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. The thing that I found really valuable is just on Wednesday mornings and Friday mornings, I just have this huge block called deep work time. If you book a time during this time, I'll slap you. And I don't know if I'm allowed to put that into meeting calendar invites anymore, but that actually worked really well. Nobody really booked meetings in that slot.
turns.zh: 不错。我发现周三和周五的早晨特别有价值，我会把这段时间称为深度工作时间。如果有人在这段时间预约会议，我会直接拒绝。我不知道现在还能不能在日程邀请里加上这个功能，但之前效果很好。没人会在这个时段预约会议。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: I didn't know Zoom had a slot feature that's coming handy.
turns.zh: 我不知道 Zoom 还有这个功能功能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It was a Google, it was in the calendar. It was like the calendar invite. And I also worked usually at least one day a week and I found that to be really effective and I know a lot of people don't want to be doing that, but I found that really important to have great success. (00:54:30): One other question along these lines around just optimizing for processing and getting stuff done and deep work time, do you have any other best practices for just being organized and staying on top of stuff, knowing there's just stuff coming at you all day every day?
turns.zh: 这是在谷歌日历上设置的。就像日历邀请一样。我通常每周至少有一天进行深度工作，发现这样效率很高。我知道很多人不愿意这样做，但我发现这对取得成功很重要。（00:54:30）：关于优化处理效率、完成任务和深度工作时间的其他最佳实践，你还有什么建议吗？特别是如何保持条理清晰、掌控进度，毕竟每天都有各种事情找上门来。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: If you're a manager and, like me, you're in back-to-back meetings from 10:00 to 6:00, it's very easy to be completely overwhelmed with a sheer amount of stuff you need to do. And so I've invested over time in just a very robust but fairly simple task management process, which is, at the end of every meeting, I would write down the tasks that I owe and the tasks that someone else owes and I would write them down to as clearly as possible, not some vague thing, but a very clear thing and just when I need to get this done by. I don't spend time just grooming. So at the end of the day, I use notes. I have just a page-long thing of all the things I need to get done, all the things people need to get done for me. And then I spend time grooming, which is basically just trying to group things together in logical chunks, grouping the tactical versus the strategic, the important versus the less important. (00:55:40): I group also what other people owe me and I Slack them what they owe me and I put a reminder on Slack for when they owe it to me by. And that way, it's just out of sight, out of mind. I think that the high-level theme is I try to create or free up headspace for processing, not memory. And so I just basically spend very little time memorizing anything and I write everything down. That is hard when you're trying to remember a specific date or remember something that someone said, but you have a system by which you can pull these things up very, very quickly. In the Google Space, you can pull up any document and search a bunch of documents very, very quickly. So that's what I would do is just spend a lot more time on the processing, be extremely good at just task management, and then grouping things, and then the next day, creating your calendar aligned to the goals that you've set for yourself the day before in terms of the tactical, where you group those tactical tasks together and then the more strategic deep thinking, walking out that additional space.
turns.zh: 假如你是一位管理者，和我一样，从上午10点到下午6点连续开会，很容易被堆积如山的工作压得喘不过气来。因此，我逐渐形成了一套既实用又简单的任务管理流程：每次会议结束后，我会把自己需要完成的任务和他人分配的任务清晰地记录下来——不是含糊其辞，而是条理分明，明确每个任务的截止日期。我不会花时间去死记硬背。一天结束时，我会把所有待办事项写在一页纸上，包括我需要完成的任务和他人为我分配的任务。然后，我会花时间进行任务分类，将战术性任务与战略性任务、重要任务与次要任务分门别类。（00:55:40）我还会在Slack上@相关人员，提醒他们完成任务的截止时间。这样一来，所有待办事项就不会被遗忘了。我认为关键在于为处理任务创造或腾出空间，而不是依赖记忆力。因此，我很少死记硬背任何内容，而是将所有信息记录下来。当需要回忆某个具体日期或某人说过的话时，系统能快速帮我调取相关信息。在Google Space中，用户可以快速搜索并调取任何文档。基于此，我的做法是投入更多精力处理任务，精通任务管理和任务分类，然后在次日根据前一天设定的战术目标调整日程，将战术任务整合起来，再进行更具战略性的深度思考，释放更多创造力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like you and I are very aligned on a lot of things. That's exactly how I approach priorities. Have you read Getting Things Done by David Allen?
turns.zh: 我觉得你和我在很多方面看法一致。这正是我处理优先事项的方式。你读过大卫·艾伦的《尽管如此，首要任务仍要完成》吗？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: I don't read a lot of nonfiction actually.
turns.zh: 实际上我不怎么读非虚构类书籍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, because what you're describing is very aligned with this approach to processing and taking to-dos, and it's what I built my approach on. And so you naturally merged out of your head. I love it. (00:57:03): Let's move on to talking a little bit about your team and hiring and things like that. And there's just going to be a grab bag set of questions. What is your current PM team look like, either number wise or just ratio and just a PM wise?
turns.zh: 好的，因为你描述的处理任务和管理待办事项的方法与我的方法非常契合，而我的方法正是基于此构建的。所以你自然而然地把它融入了你的思维中。我很喜欢。（00:57:03）接下来让我们聊聊你的团队、招聘等话题。问题会比较随机。你们目前的PM团队是什么样的？无论是人数还是比例，或者仅从PM的角度来看？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: We have about 13 PMs at Ramp and probably over a hundred engineers. So I try to keep basically one to eight to one to 15 depending on the team. Obviously, B2B is slightly more complex because you're dealing with pretty strong marketing team and pretty strong sales team and pretty demanding customers that you have relationships with. So I've seen ratios be a bit lower than the B2C space. But, yeah, that's a little bit of the team today. And they're organized by those teams, by those customer pain points.
turns.zh: Ramp目前有大约13位PM，可能还有超过100位工程师。所以我尽量保持PM与工程师的比例在1比8到1比15之间，具体取决于团队情况。显然，B2B领域要稍微复杂一些，因为你需要应对强大的营销团队、强大的销售团队，以及与客户建立关系的要求很高的客户群体。所以我发现B2C领域的PM比例会稍低一些。不过，嗯，这就是我们目前团队的情况。他们按照这些团队、这些客户痛点进行组织。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I have this note from before, you said that you reached a hundred million ARR, and that's a run rate, not recurring revenue at that point, I imagine, right?
turns.zh: 我之前看到你提到达到1亿美元的ARR，这应该是营收预测，而不是实际收入，对吧？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With 50 people, which is incredible. And so just on that point, how do you do so much with so few PMs, especially? Do you have anything that you figured out that ends up being really important there?
turns.zh: 有50个人，这真是令人惊叹。说到这一点，你们是如何用如此少的产品经理来完成如此多的工作的，尤其是？你们有没有发现什么非常重要的方法？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: I think that by eliminating or reducing the size of the team, we've forced other people in the company to think like PMs and I think it's been a huge value add to our culture. When I say product, often people think about product management, but I actually think product is anyone that actually reports into our CTO, and that's product engineering, product design, product managers, product data scientists. So making everyone feel like a PM is a great way to get leverage as a PM, and that means basically empowering the designer to think about the actual specs and priorities and scopes more than you or empower the engineer to take something that's fairly lightweight in terms of a spec or direction and actually think through it deeply and come back with some great questions that the PM hasn't thought through. So that's one thing. (00:58:58): The second is that we invested early on in product operations, which was a team that also reports to me that basically focuses on the operational functions of product that's everything around whether it's project management or issue management or release management or enablement and content beta and customer research. They basically are tasked with a lot of the work that needs to get done to continue shipping products and scaling product development. (00:59:29): And then lastly, just cutting as much of the low-leverage work that PMs often get sucked into. So, for example, we never write a ticket. We don't spend much time in linear, which is our ticket management system. Basically, our contract is the vision and the priority and a very high-level spec and everything else is pushed on the engineering teams. And I think that's when engineers actually are also able to move even faster because they can create whatever tickets they want, they can break down the work that they want, they are accountable for the projects that they're driving, and that increases trust and moves things faster as well.
turns.zh: 我认为，通过减少或消除团队规模，我们迫使公司其他人像产品经理一样思考问题，我认为这对我们的文化产生了巨大的增值效应。当我说产品时，很多人会想到产品管理，但实际上我认为产品是指向我们的CTO汇报的任何人，包括产品工程、产品设计、产品经理、产品数据科学家。所以让每个人都感觉自己像产品经理，是作为产品经理获得杠杆的好方法，这基本上意味着赋予设计师权力，使他们能够更多地考虑实际的规格、优先级和范围，而不是你来考虑；或者赋予工程师权力，使他们能够更深入地思考一个规格或方向相当轻量的东西，并提出一些产品经理没有想到的好问题。所以这是一方面。（00:58:58）：第二方面是，我们很早就投资了产品运营团队，这个团队也向我汇报，主要关注产品的运营功能，包括项目管理、问题管理、发布管理、赋能和内容测试，以及客户研究。他们基本上负责所有需要完成的工作，以继续推出产品并扩展产品开发。（00:59:29）：最后，减少产品经理常被卷入的低效工作。例如，我们从不写工单，也不花太多时间在我们的工单管理系统Linearly上。基本上，我们的合同是愿景和优先级，以及一个非常高层次的规格，其他一切都推给工程团队。我认为这就是为什么工程师实际上能够更快地行动，因为他们可以创建任何他们想要的工单，他们可以分解他们想要的工作，对于他们推动的项目，他们负有责任，这增加了信任，也让事情进展得更快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes a ton of sense. Basically, you distribute the PM job that other companies put on the PM across other team members. So if you had to think about just what is the core product manager job at Ramp at this point, I imagine from what I've been hearing, it's strategy, vision, aligning the team. What else plays into that, just bullet point wise? A few things that come to mind.
turns.zh: 这太有道理了。基本上，你们把其他公司交给产品经理的工作，分散到了其他团队成员身上。那么，如果你必须思考Ramp产品经理的核心职责是什么，我想从我听到的来看，就是战略、愿景、团队协作。还有哪些方面呢？简要列出几点。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Team building. So building a culture within the pod because oftentimes your managers are no longer in your team, right? Engineers might report to different people, designers might report to different people. PMs might report to different people. So actually building a team culture within the pod is really, really important. And oftentimes it falls on the PM to create those offsites or to create those ideation sessions or to find ways to have fun as a team. (01:01:00): The second is making sure that the team is humming in terms of the actual focus areas and then protecting the team from stakeholders that might want to have an opinion or want to have an update or want to schedule certain meetings. So protecting that core team from that chaos and then being the central point of contact if someone has a question or needs something, and then being able to bring in the right person at the right time. So those are the different things that is also really important to mention.
turns.zh:
团队建设。所以，要在团队内部营造一种文化氛围，因为很多时候你的经理们不再在你的团队里了，对吧？工程师可能会向不同的人汇报，设计师可能会向不同的人汇报。产品经理可能会向不同的人汇报。所以，实际上在团队内部建立一种团队文化真的非常非常重要。而这项任务往往就落在了产品经理的肩上，比如组织团队外出活动、开展头脑风暴会议，或者想办法让团队玩得开心。
（01:01:00）第二点是，确保团队在实际的重点领域上保持高效运作，同时还要保护团队免受那些想插嘴、想获取进展更新、想安排会议的干扰因素的打扰。因此，要保护核心团队免受这些混乱的干扰，并成为团队的核心联络人。如果有人有问题或需要帮助，你要能够在恰当的时间找到合适的人来解决问题。所以，这些都是非常重要且值得提及的要点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to a note that I made earlier, you talked about how a lot of this advice you're sharing in the approach to product at Ramp is assuming that the team is A plus, the engineers are A plus, the designers A plus. For somebody listening to this that may be wondering, "Are my engineers A plus or not?", what comes to mind as ways that you could get a sense of this is a team that can operate in this way versus, no, we're never going to work in this way and maybe we should shift the way we work or I should get work somewhere else?
turns.zh: 回到我之前提到的观点，你提到在Ramp公司，你分享的很多产品开发方法都假设团队成员都是顶尖人才，工程师是顶尖的，设计师也是顶尖的。对于听众来说，他们可能会想：“我的团队成员是顶尖的吗？”。那么，如何判断团队是否具备这样的能力呢？比如，团队是否能够以这种高效的方式运作？还是说，我们永远无法达到这种标准，或许我们应该调整工作方式？又或者我应该换一家公司工作？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Great question. Yeah, it's very hard to identify. A few things. One is, does the engineer want to win in the market? Does the engineer really care about winning against competitors, winning the hearts and minds of the customer? Do they understand the business context in which they operate by which they need to do that? Are they curious about how the company makes money, about what customers love and don't love, about what the most important project is and why it's important? They're asking you questions about the business outside of just the engineering domains. Are they able to execute on what they said they were going to execute without your help or do you actually feel like you need to be behind them? Are they the one actually setting the pace, asking you to keep up with your specs, keep up with your decisions, respond more quickly to the things that are blocking them, bringing more PMs or more designers to do more things? (01:03:14): Are they being proactive in different channels where you think it's actually your job, but actually they'll jump in anyways? For example, we have different Slack channels with a bunch of people sometimes asking questions or raising issues or having blockers. And you have engineers who are just jumping in and explaining how a feature works, getting the feedback and fixing a bug proactively. And you may think, "Well, that's not the priority. I need to control what the engineers are doing." That's not your job actually, that's not your job. Your job is to make sure that they're aligned with the long-term vision and that they can deliver what they've committed to, but on top of that, they can do whatever the hell they want. And if they're taking on something that puts the things that they committed to at risk, they'll communicate that. So, again, that proactiveness, that desire to help, that desire to improve that accountability on their product. (01:04:03): If their product isn't performing, if their product has feedback, are they doing it themselves or they need you to push them? So those are all mentality and culture aspects. I'm not even getting into the technical rigor and the quality of their systems and the velocity of code because I'm not a good judge of that. That's not really my role. But those are the things that I would immediately look at that, I think, is just fundamentally different in the engineering team that we built at Ramp versus others. And it's just a big part of the culture shift and the culture that we've been able to build.
turns.zh: 好问题。这确实很难判断。关键有几个方面。首先，工程师是否想在市场上取胜？他们是否真的在乎战胜竞争对手、赢得客户的心？他们是否理解所在业务环境的需求，从而达成这些目标？他们是否对公司的盈利模式、客户的喜好与痛点、最重要的项目及其重要性充满好奇？他们会问一些工程领域之外的业务问题，是否能在没有你帮助的情况下执行既定计划，还是你觉得必须时刻监督他们？他们是否在主动设定节奏，要求你跟上技术规范、决策进度，迅速解决阻碍进展的问题，引入更多产品经理或设计师来完成更多工作？（01:03:14）他们是否在你认为本应由你负责的不同渠道上积极行动？比如，我们有多个Slack频道，大家时常在那里提问、反馈问题或报告阻碍因素。有些工程师会主动介入，解释某个功能的运作原理，收集反馈并主动修复漏洞。你可能会想：“这不是优先事项，我需要管控工程师的工作。”但这其实不是你的职责。你的职责是确保他们与长期愿景保持一致，交付承诺成果之余，还能自由发挥。若他们的行动危及既定目标，他们会主动沟通。再比如，他们的主动性、帮助欲望、产品责任心等文化特质。（01:04:03）若产品表现不佳、有用户反馈，他们是自己解决还是需要你督促？这些都是思维模式和文化层面的考量。我暂不评判技术严谨性、系统质量或开发效率，因为我对此不甚擅长，这并非我的职责范畴。但这些正是Ramp团队与其他工程团队存在根本差异的关键所在，也是我们成功构建的文化转型的核心要素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was an awesome answer. And I think as a PM, you often don't want your engineers and designers to have such strong opinions and to be so on top of everything because there's just like, "Oh, no. Okay, here's what I think we should actually do," but engineers have all these opinions. And what you're saying is that's what you want to lean into, assuming you trust that they know what they're doing and can actually get things done. And so it's like a catchment to you a little bit, but I think that's a really unique culture and approach. And so that's an awesome answer.
turns.zh: 这真是个精彩的回答。我觉得作为产品经理，往往不希望工程师和设计师有太强的主见、对一切了如指掌，因为总会出现“哦，不行，还是按我说的来”的情况，但工程师们总有各种看法。你说这正是你希望鼓励的，前提是信任他们的专业能力和执行力。所以这对我们来说是个挑战，但我认为这是一种独特的文化和方法。真是很棒的回答。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: And, look, there's drawbacks to that culture where you get to a radically empowered engineering team that thinks that they know the product better than the designer or the PM and they push back on the designs or they disagree with the PM, but I'll take that culture any day compared to a culture where they're just taking things at face value and not challenging the thinking and not actually thinking from their own perspectives. And it is like I'll take someone on my team any day that challenges what I tell them to do or what I think is important and is maybe a bit harder to manage, but it'll make me think way deeper about what I'm asking them and what I think is important. And I'll grow as a manager much faster because of that.
turns.zh: 看吧，这种文化也有弊端——当你拥有一支极具权力的工程团队时，他们会认为自己比设计师或产品经理更懂产品，反驳设计方案或质疑产品经理的决策。但比起那种人们只按字面意思行事、不质疑现有思维、也不从自身视角思考的文化，我宁愿选择前者。我愿意接受团队中那些挑战我指令、质疑我优先事项的人，虽然他们可能更难管理，但这能让我更深入地思考自己的要求和优先事项。正因如此，我作为管理者的成长速度会快得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. Two final questions, one around hiring. When you're interviewing people, what do you look for and what does Ramp look for that maybe other companies don't value as much as they should or maybe overvalue? What do you look for that you think is unique that helps you hire this A-plus team?
turns.zh: 太棒了。最后两个问题，第一个关于招聘。在面试候选人时，您最看重什么？Ramp在招聘时又关注哪些方面，而其他公司可能没有给予足够重视或存在过度重视的情况？您认为哪些独特的品质有助于招到顶尖人才？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: We look for people who have a very strong desire to have impact. And the best way to assess that is the impact that they've had or the reason why they are switching jobs. So, again, it goes back to what I was mentioning earlier in the chat, which was velocity leads to people wanting to join because they want to have velocity. And the best signal that is, I'm leaving because things got too slow, things got too bureaucratic. I missed the old days where we were just building and shipping and launching. I look for people who can think deeply, so I'll go super deep into a decision, a tradeoff that they had to make. And I'll really just scratch at that until I get to a deep understanding of how they make decisions and how deep they think about things. (01:06:57): And in general, we tend to overemphasize those two skills rather than necessarily experience because experience ... Again, to the point around Ramp is a unique business, it matters a lot less. You can have a lot less impact than your ability to be hungry and your ability to think deeply.
turns.zh: 我们寻找那些渴望产生影响力的人。而评估这一点的最佳方式，就是看他们过去产生的影响或跳槽的原因。正如我之前在聊天中提到的，速度感能吸引人才，因为人们渴望在快节奏中工作。最典型的信号是，离职原因可能是进展太慢、流程太繁琐。他们怀念过去那种专注于开发、上线和发布的时光。我还关注候选人能否深度思考问题——比如深入探讨他们曾面临的决策权衡。我会不断追问，直到完全理解他们的决策逻辑和思考深度。（01:06:57）总的来说，我们更看重这两项能力，而非经验，因为经验……回到Ramp的独特之处——经验的重要性远不及求知欲和深度思考能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. A lot of people listening to this want to get into product management. What's your advice? I'm sure you get asked this a lot. How do you break into product management? What do you tell people?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。很多听众都想进入产品管理领域，您有什么建议？我相信您常被问到这个问题。如何进入产品管理领域？您会给出怎样的建议？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Yeah. So for me, I went from college to consulting to my four into tech was really into more like solutions analyst, I think that was my title. I was basically trying to implement a large B2B software in national banks. And how I got into product management was really around understanding deeply the customer and understanding deeply the product and being able to show impact on the combination of these two things. Typically, the folks that join product teams are the highest performers outside of product that either understand the customer really well and can advise product or understand the product very well and can serve customers. (01:08:12): And so my advice is for folks that want to break into that is to find a role that is adjacent to product that enables you to have those experiences and to prove yourself. So, for example, product operations is a good one. Business operations is a good one. More consulting sales engineering or solution engineering is a good one. There are designers and engineers that can become PMs as well. Typically, it's folks that can do the job as well as the PM. And what we typically do is we give those PMs a shot or those folks a shot. So we'd give them like six months to go into a new area and try it out. And then we basically have the engineers they work with and designers they work with actually make the call as to whether or not they would want this PM versus another PM on the team.
turns.zh:
是的。对我来说，我从大学到咨询公司，再到科技行业，起初担任的是解决方案分析师。我主要负责在全国性银行中实施大型B2B软件。后来我如何转入产品管理领域，主要在于深入理解客户需求和产品特性，并能证明这两者的结合能产生实际效果。我们通常会让那些在产品团队之外表现出色的人加入，比如对客户有深刻理解并能为产品提供建议的人，或者对产品有深入了解并能服务客户的人。

（01:08:12）所以我的建议是，如果想进入产品管理领域，可以先找一个与产品相邻的角色，让你获得相关经验并证明自己的能力。例如，产品运营是一个不错的选择。业务运营也是不错的选择。更多的咨询、销售工程或解决方案工程也是不错的选择。设计师和工程师也可以成为产品经理。通常，他们需要既能胜任产品经理的工作，又能胜任其他工作。我们通常会给这些产品经理一个机会，或者让他们尝试新领域六个月。然后，他们的工程师和设计师同事会决定是否要选择这位产品经理而不是团队中的其他人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else you want to share before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, first, think from first principles, don't take everything I'm saying at face value. And second is back to talent, that a huge part of our success was the early team that Karim built on the tech side. And so I can write blogs all day on how we increased velocity, but if there's one thing to take away from this is that empowered and talented engineers and designers are the biggest reason why Ramp was so successful and it's something that requires a ton of focus. I mean, early on for the first year at Ramp, Karim, our CTO, was only focused on that. It was hiring the best talent. He was a lot less interested or focused on our product strategy, our product market fit, or even our revenue. It was all about bringing in the best engineers and the best designers and that has had compounding effects on the company and the team.
turns.zh: 是的。首先，基于基本原则，不要把我说的话都当真。其次，再次强调人才的重要性，我们成功的很大一部分原因在于Karim在技术部门组建的早期团队。因此，我可以整天写博客讲述我们如何提高开发效率，但最重要的一点是，赋予有才华的工程师和设计师权力是Ramp成功的最大原因，这一点需要高度关注。例如，在Ramp成立的第一年，Karim，我们的CTO，只专注于招聘最优秀的人才。他对我们的产品策略、产品市场匹配度甚至收入都兴趣不大，一心只想引进最优秀的工程师和设计师，这对公司和团队产生了连锁反应。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think an important element there is the initial people you hire end up impacting the next batch and the next set because they see, "Wow, this person is working at Ramp. That's incredible. I got to look at that." So there's an early compounding effect, too, that happens.
turns.zh: 我认为一个重要的因素是，你最初招聘的人最终会影响后续的团队，因为他们会看到：“哇，这个人在Ramp工作，这太棒了。我得看看。”所以这也产生了早期的连锁反应。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好的，接下来是激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有六个问题要问你，你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你向其他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Because I work a lot, I try to read things that are completely outside of work. I don't think I can get through any fiction or nonfiction book that's often recommended. So anything that will pull on your heartstrings and try to make you more human. When Breath Becomes Air is a really good one that I often recommend.
turns.zh: 因为我工作很忙，所以我尽量读一些与工作完全无关的书。我觉得我读不完那些常被推荐的小说或非小说类书籍。所以任何能触动你心弦、试图让你更人性化的书。我经常推荐《当呼吸化作空气》这本书，真的很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Love that one. Favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我超爱这部剧。最近看过的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: I started watching The Bear a few weeks ago. I think it's a great show around leadership around how a different industry operates, the restaurant industry. My dad owned a restaurant so I got a little bit into that and all about teamwork and quality versus velocity [inaudible 01:11:24] of personal and professional stress. So I thought it was a really good learning.
turns.zh: 几周前我开始看《熊大厨》。我觉得这部剧很棒，它讲的是不同行业——餐饮业的领导力，以及团队合作和质量与效率的平衡，还有个人和职业压力的问题。所以我觉得这部剧能带来很好的启发。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that show makes me really think of Ramp. That makes a lot of sense. It feels very ... Everything's just crazy moving fast. I'm just so stressed watching that show. I haven't watched the second season yet.
turns.zh: 哇，这部剧让我想起了《Ramp》。这太有道理了。感觉一切都疯狂地快速运转。我看这部剧的时候压力好大。我还没看第二季呢。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: You should come to our office, probably very similar.
turns.zh: 你应该来我们公司看看，可能很相似。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just delicious food, sandwiches and the velocity. Favorite interview question you'd like to ask candidates?
turns.zh: 就是美味的食物、三明治和高效率。最喜欢问候选人的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: I ask, what's the hardest thing you've ever done? And I ask that because working at Ramp is hard. I want to understand what hard means for them. I want to understand why it was hard. I want to understand how they overcame that difficulty, how they worked with other people to overcome that difficulty, and how much agency they had in overcoming that. So it's a really good sign around what is difficult to them and how much work they put into overcoming that.
turns.zh: 我会问：你做过的最困难的事是什么？我这么问是因为在Ramp工作很不容易。我想了解对他们来说什么是困难的，为什么困难，以及他们如何克服困难，如何与他人合作克服困难，还有他们在克服困难时有多强的主动性。这样就能很好地了解对他们来说什么是困难的，以及他们为克服困难付出了多少努力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 最近发现的最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: So my partner bought me this WHOOP recently. Wearing it now. It gives you this real-time stress signal. [inaudible 01:12:36] that's pretty helpful. But I think it's a great product in terms of just actual insights. It's very data-driven, so it'll tell you ... You have a daily journal of all the things you did that day and it'll correlate what you did that day to your recovery score or how healthy you are for that day. (01:12:55): And so it'll give you insights around how certain actions you take will have impact on your next day's health, which is all about heart rate variability. I thought it was just a great way to continue to focus on your health. I think running a team has a huge impact on your physical health, on your mental health, and I think you are an athlete at a high growth startup or even a small business or a large company. And focusing on that health is really, really important. So any tools like the WHOOP to invest into that is great.
turns.zh: 我搭档最近给我买了这个WHOOP。我现在戴着它。它能实时监测你的压力水平。[01:12:36]这太有用了。但从数据驱动的角度来看，它的产品设计很棒。它会记录你一天的活动，并将这些活动与你的恢复分数或当天健康状况相关联。（01:12:55）这样就能让你了解某些行为对第二天健康的影响，这都与心率变异性有关。我觉得这真是关注健康的好方法。管理团队对你的身体健康和心理健康都有巨大影响。无论是在高增长的初创公司，还是小企业或大公司，关注健康都非常重要。所以像WHOOP这样的工具投资很值得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was a really good pitch for the WHOOP. I have never wanted one, but now I do. Okay, next question. What is something relatively minor you've changed in your product development process that has had a big impact on your team's ability to execute?
turns.zh: 你对WHOOP的介绍真不错。我之前从没想买，但现在有兴趣了。下一个问题。你在产品开发流程中做了哪些相对小的改进，却对团队执行能力产生了重大影响？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: It's not something I've changed, it's more something that our head of design, Diego, has changed. Basically having designers spend more time creating more visionary prototypes and then sharing those out in videos. It just has just huge impact on how exciting work is and how excited the team are. And so just providing that clarity is massive. And I think just, again, Figma and Loom and prototypes that actually are interactive so people can actually play around with it is a huge way to unlock velocity.
turns.zh: 这不是我做的，而是我们的设计主管迭戈做的。基本上，让设计师花更多时间创作更具远见的原型，然后用视频分享出来。这样对激发团队的工作热情和兴奋感有巨大影响。所以提供这种清晰度非常重要。我觉得再说一次，Figma和Loom，以及能让人们实际操作的互动原型，是释放效率的绝佳方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. I've already asked you about this a couple of times, but I'm curious if there's any other productivity tip or tool that you'd recommend to listeners that you haven't mentioned yet.
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。我已经问过你几次了，但我很好奇，你有没有什么其他提高效率的技巧或工具想推荐给听众，而我们之前还没提到过？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Turn off notifications. Quit Slack when you're doing deep work. Check your emails once a day and just literally go through them in five minutes. Oftentimes, most of them use lists. Check Slack only at the top of the hour. Use Slack snooze or reminders. I mean, there's a whole other podcast we can talk about over Slack channels and how to organize that, but just get really good at the tools you're using. I think the first year of consulting, we just got really good at Excel and Excel shortcuts, and it was a big part of our training. And so just train yourself and train your teams on how to use their tools, how to use your calendar, how to use Slack, how to use email, whatever the tool you've designed as the right tool for you. Be dogmatic. I mean, what Ramp is, is a tool at the end of the day and we're helping finance teams more efficient, so let's dock through that and do that with our own tools.
turns.zh: 关闭通知。当你需要专心工作时，退出Slack。每天只查看一次邮件，五分钟快速浏览即可。通常，大多数邮件都是列表形式的。每小时整点再查看Slack。使用Slack的延迟提醒或通知功能。我的意思是，我们可以专门做一期播客，聊聊如何组织Slack频道，但首先要把现有工具用好。我记得咨询业务的第一年，我们就把Excel和Excel快捷键练得炉火纯青，这也是我们培训的重要内容。所以，要训练自己和团队如何使用工具、日历、Slack，以及任何你设计的合适工具。保持原则性。我觉得Ramp本质上就是一个工具，我们致力于帮助财务团队提高效率，所以就专注于此，用好自己的工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think we've had just enough velocity in our chat. I think we're going to hit a hundred million downloads. I think we built an A-plus team here. Geoff, thank you so much for doing this. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to ask you any other questions? And second question, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 我觉得我们的聊天互动已经足够热烈了。我们的下载量即将达到一亿次。我觉得我们组建了一支A+团队。杰夫，非常感谢你参与这次访谈。最后两个问题。如果听众想继续提问，可以在哪里找到你？第二个问题，听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: You can find me on Twitter and LinkedIn. Twitter is geoffintech. How can they be useful? Honestly, your attention is a gift. If you're interested in joining us here at Ramp, we're obviously hiring incredible people. So if anything that I shared resonates with you and if you want to join the team, and we're hiring across product engineering design, but most importantly, be kind to yourself. I think I've been a huge listener to this podcast. It's an honor to be here. I know very little. Hopefully some of what I shared was meaningful to you. But keep the growth mindset. Keep thinking from first principles. Keep investing in that growth and be patient. It takes a lot of time.
turns.zh: 你可以在Twitter和LinkedIn上找到我。Twitter账号是geoffintech。如何提供帮助呢？说实话，你的关注就是一份礼物。如果你有兴趣加入Ramp，我们显然在招募优秀人才。所以，如果我分享的观点能引起你的共鸣，并且你想加入团队，我们在产品工程、设计等多个岗位招人，但最重要的是，要善待自己。我一直是这个播客的忠实听众。很荣幸能来这里分享。我知道自己懂得不多，但希望我分享的部分能对你有所启发。保持成长型思维，从第一性原理出发，不断投资自我成长，保持耐心。这需要时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a beautiful way to end it. Geoff, thank you again so much for being here.
turns.zh: 多么美好的收尾方式。杰夫，再次感谢你的到来。

turns.speaker: Geoff Charles
turns.en: Thanks a lot, Lenny. This was a lot of fun.
turns.zh: 非常感谢，莱尼。这次交流非常愉快。
